en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī, while wandering for alms in a certain street in Sāvatthī, approached a certain family; having approached, she sat down on a seat prepared for her.
Then those people, having fed that bhikkhunī, said this:
"May other bhikkhunīs also come, noble lady."
Then that bhikkhunī, thinking, "How can it be that the bhikkhunīs do not come? approached the bhikkhunīs and said this:
"Venerable ladies, in such-and-such a place there are wild dogs, a fierce ox, and the ground is muddy."
"Do not go there.
Then another bhikkhunī, while wandering for alms in that street, approached that family; having approached, she sat down on the prepared seat.
Then those people, having fed that bhikkhunī, said this to her:
“Why, noble lady, are the bhikkhunīs not coming?
Then that bhikkhunī explained the matter to those people.
The people criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“How indeed can a bhikkhunī be stingy toward a family?
… [as before] … “Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī is stingy toward a family?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, monks, can a bhikkhunī be stingy toward a family?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule thus:
“Whichever nun should be one who is miserly regarding families, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Whichever nun... [means]... “whichever nun.”
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... "bhikkhunī" ...pe...
this is the nun intended in this context.
"Family" means four kinds of families: the khattiya family, the brāhmaṇa family, the vessa family, and the sudda family.
"She would be stingy" means...
If one speaks dispraise of the family in the presence of the bhikkhunīs, thinking, "How might the bhikkhunīs not come? there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Or, if one speaks dispraise of the bhikkhunīs in the presence of the family, there is an offense of expiation.
There is no offense—
Not being stingy with her family, she points out even an existing danger;
[this is] for one who is insane,
for one who is a first-time offender.
The fifth training rule is concluded.
